p: The river rises about 140 kilometres west of Moscow, crosses Smolensk and Moscow Oblasts and reaches the Oka about 110 kilometres south-east of the capital. Its length is given as 473 kilometres, or by another measure 502, its basin covers 17,600 square kilometres, and it falls 155 metres along its course. An estimated 61 per cent of its water comes from thaw, 12 per cent from rain and 27 per cent from underground sources. It normally freezes around November or December and begins to thaw in late March. On its banks, besides Moscow, stand Mozhaysk, Zvenigorod, Zhukovsky, Bronnitsy and Voskresensk.

Recent studies suggest that the river has occupied its present bed for about 12,000 years. Finnic peoples lived along it, as did Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi. The name of the city is thought to come from that of the river. The most widely accepted explanation derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root connected with wetness, so that it may have meant a river in a marsh or wetland. One Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds instead that the Merya and Muroma, pre-Slavic peoples of the area, called it Mustajoki, black river. To tell the two apart, Russians usually call the river Moskva-reka.

The first stone bridge across it, the Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, was built in 1692. The Vodootvodny Canal, dug in the 1780s, created the island opposite the Kremlin that Muscovites informally call Bolotny Ostrov, Bog Island. Dams built in 1785, 1836 and 1878 failed to keep the river navigable through summer droughts. The highest recorded water level in central Moscow, 127.25 metres above sea level against a usual 120, was reached in the flood of 1908.

Since the Moscow Canal was completed, in 1932–1937, the river has also carried a share of water from the upper Volga, which has made commercial shipping reliable. The average discharge, Volga water included, rises from 38 cubic metres a second near Zvenigorod to 250 at the mouth. As of 2007 there were 49 bridges over the river and its canals within the city, where it is 120 to 200 metres wide and narrowest under the Kremlin walls. Moscow draws its drinking water from five stations on the river and from the upper Volga reservoirs. The stretch within the city freezes only occasionally, on account of contamination.

notes: The article's history section is two sentences; the History section here leans on its etymology and scattered dated facts.
The article gives two lengths (473 or 502 km); the entry says about 470.
The article's sentence 'the Moskva River is also the origin of Slavic tribes such as the Vyatichi' is loosely worded; I wrote only that they lived along it.
